source.title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
source.authors: Juncheng Ma; Jiaxin Li; Jiankai Tu; Bo Liang; Guodong Lv; Yufan Deng; Junzhe Tang; Liangzhu Yang; Chen Bian; Zicong Cao; Baohao Zhu; Jianxin Bi; Tengfei Yan; Yinyuan Zhang; Kewei Zhang; Xinglong Chen; Kaiqi Chen; Duomin Wang; Xiaotian Tang; Liang Tan; Li Li; Yuan Xu; Haosen Yang; Yuqi Wang; Jingfei Xia; Songyan Huang; Zhiyang Dou; Zhen Dong; Enze Xie; Tat-Seng Chua; Daquan Zhou

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The title in the supplied metadata differs from the title printed in the paper; the paper itself is about Open-HumanWAM.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling analysis to egocentric human-video pretraining and embodied robot-task performance. It reports scaling results in this new setting, using downstream success rather than language-model held-out loss.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter-count or token-count scaling, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its own relevant results are data-scale sweeps with robot-task success as the outcome. Other model leaderboard results and cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: No version is tested. The study scales egocentric or hybrid data for robot world–action models and fits downstream robot success linearly in log10 hours (SR = a + b log10 H). It measures no held-out pretraining loss and fits no power law in loss. It does not sweep parameters or compute (backbone fixed at 5B or 16B). It is not a language-model study. V5 names the power-law loss form in other modalities; success rate that is linear in log-hours is a different construct. V6 concerns language-model downstream tasks. These results go under fits_no_version, not version verdicts.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors report an empirical log-linear law between egocentric pretraining hours and downstream robot success, mainly out of distribution. They also report steeper trends with greater task and scene diversity, and better sample efficiency at larger scale. Hybrid scaling improves zero-shot transfer, with plateaus on some settings. Robot-balanced sampling helps on hard tasks. Note that the 'scaling law' is a success-rate log fit, not a loss power law.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales egocentric or hybrid embodied-training data and measures downstream robot-task success after post-training or in zero-shot deployment. It does not use the original language-model held-out cross-entropy measurement or sweep parameter count, tokens, and training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted success-rate slopes vary with task and scene diversity (scaled-diversity versus matched-diversity). Results also vary with attention configuration: isolated-attention clean success increases with scale, whereas IDM-attention clean success stays nearly flat. At fixed hybrid data budget, robot-balanced sampling changes hard-task success.

fits_no_version.finding: For a fixed-size robot world–action model, closed-loop RoboTwin success after post-training rises roughly linearly in log10 egocentric pretraining hours. The fits are strongest out of distribution: scene-ood R2 0.949/0.969 and random R2 0.877/0.955. In-distribution (clean) success saturates under IDM attention.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In embodied video world–action models, downstream robot task success increases log-linearly with egocentric pretraining data hours, especially under distribution shift.

fits_no_version.finding: Expanding task and scene diversity with duration gives steeper log-linear success slopes than adding duration at fixed coverage, in all three settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling slopes for embodied pretraining depend on task and scene diversity, not hours alone.

fits_no_version.finding: In robot plus human co-training, zero-shot and post-trained robot success generally rises with total data. It plateaus for robot-only Random post-training and for hard real-robot tasks. Balancing the robot/human sampling ratio at fixed data changes hard-task success from 19% to 27%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hybrid human–robot data scaling improves robot generalization, with returns that saturate and depend on the data mixture.

record.problems: The scaling outcomes are downstream robot success rates rather than held-out pretraining loss. The paper reports no error bars or confidence intervals for the scaling results. It selects the best post-training checkpoint independently for each evaluation setting, and some reported conditions show saturation or plateaus.
record.rows_left_out: Left out detailed sample-efficiency results in Section 3.4, additional multi-view and action-alignment ablations in Sections 3.5–3.8 and 4.4, and task-level hybrid scaling breakdowns in Figures 18 and 21; these are secondary to the central scale-versus-success findings. Also left out RoboTwin leaderboard comparisons and real-robot goal-conditioning demonstrations because they do not report a distinct scaling relationship relevant to the claim.

untested.parts: No held-out loss; no parameter, token or compute sweep; no language models.
No extrapolation of small-run loss fits to larger runs. Authors only say the trends 'suggest' further gains.
No compute-optimal parameter/data allocation; model size is fixed.
No depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count. The attention-mask ablations change information flow, not shape.
Video/robot models are studied, but no pretraining-loss power law is fitted. Outcomes are success rates fitted linearly in log-hours.
No language-model downstream tasks and no performance-versus-pretraining-loss relation.
No comparison of loss-law fitting choices, parameter counting or schedule effects on fitted exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests and its V5/V6/V7 labels are removed. The study is outside the language-model claim: it uses no loss power law and varies no parameters or compute. Caveats for anyone reusing the fits: batch size grows with corpus size, and the best checkpoint is chosen separately per evaluation setting, which can inflate the fits. No error bars are reported. The robot-versus-egocentric pretraining scaling series (Fig. 12, 100–5k h) is not in the rows. It would belong with the fits_no_version findings if extracted. Metadata title mismatch noted.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
The study does not fit small-run language-model loss curves and test their predictions on much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts is conducted.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Tests scaling in egocentric video pretraining and human–robot co-training using downstream robot performance, not the original held-out language-model loss measure. Other modalities and regimes such as image/video generation loss, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer beyond robot manipulation are not tested.
Tests downstream robot success and task coverage against pretraining data scale, not downstream language-model tasks or performance against pretraining loss.

Examines dependence of downstream-success scaling fits on data diversity and attention configuration. It does not test parameter counting, compute-optimal allocations, language-model loss fitting choices, or systematic bending of language-model loss curves.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Egocentric human-video pretraining and human–robot co-training for robot manipulation
reader_labels.reason: The study reports log-linear downstream-success scaling with egocentric hours and higher zero-shot robot success as human data are added; this is evidence in an embodied setting, not evidence about language-model loss. Rows R1–R3, R5–R6, R16, R19–R21.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pure egocentric scaling under scene-ood and random evaluation, and hybrid scaling in zero-shot simulation and real-robot tasks
reader_labels.reason: Success and task coverage generally improve with pretraining data scale, including reported high-fit log-linear relationships for out-of-distribution RoboTwin settings. Rows R2–R3, R5–R6, R15–R16, R19–R21.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Clean evaluation with IDM attention; hard-task physical zero-shot evaluation; robot-only post-training scale
reader_labels.reason: Clean success changes little over 100–50,000 hours, hard-task gains plateau from 30,519 to 60,556 total hours under standard sampling, and robot-only Random post-training success plateaus from 8,475 to 14,618 hours. Rows R4, R18, R20.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: EgoSuite scaling with expanding versus fixed task and scene coverage
reader_labels.reason: The fitted slopes vary with the data-coverage construction: expanding diversity produces steeper slopes than duration scaling at fixed coverage in all three evaluation settings. Rows R7–R12.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Hard-task physical zero-shot evaluation at a fixed 60,556-hour budget
reader_labels.reason: Changing the human-to-robot sampling ratio changes hard-task success from 19.0% to 27.0%, showing sensitivity to training-mixture choice. Row R22.
